item.title: Limtiaco, Moylan outline differing approaches in congressional debate

item.content:encoded:
Alicia Limtiaco and Del. James Moylan outlined their priorities for Guam during a Guam Chamber of Commerce congressional debate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

Both candidates said Guam needs relief from high living costs, better access to federal funding and benefits, stronger infrastructure, and more economic opportunities. Both candidates also supported addressing the Jones Act’s impact on Guam’s shipping costs, expanding air service and competition, improving access to federal benefits, and returning unused federal land for local use. However, they offered different approaches to addressing those concerns.

Limtiaco, a former Guam attorney general and U.S. attorney, said her campaign would focus on fairness for Guam in federal programs, accountability for government spending, and creating more opportunities for local businesses and workers.

Limtiaco said she would push for more affordable housing by helping restore vacant or deteriorating homes through existing federal housing programs. To improve accountability, Limtiaco proposed tracking federal funding and project progress through public updates, as well as using congressional hearings and oversight to address delays or misuse of funds.

“I will establish a Guam Business and Economic Advisory Council to bring your experience into our congressional office, and I will report back on what has moved, what funding has been approved, and where work remains,” Limtiaco said.

Moylan emphasized his record in Congress and the federal funding and legislation he said he has helped secure for Guam. He said he would continue working to reduce barriers for local businesses, expand workforce opportunities, and pursue changes to shipping and air travel policies.

“These are real investments in the safety and well-being of our people, and I welcome the scrutiny,” Moylan said. “My commitment to serving you began long before this election. I served through the pandemic, through the devastation of Typhoon Mawar, and challenges that followed. Public service is a responsibility.”

On shipping, Moylan said he has introduced measures seeking exemptions from the Jones Act for Guam, including for fuel and emergencies. He said he would continue pushing a permanent exemption, while Limtiaco called for a broader review of how the law affects Guam and what changes would best address the island’s needs.

“I have already introduced with Congressman Ed Case from Hawaii over 11 measures that address the Jones Act exception specifically for Guam regarding fuel, regarding emergency situations,” Moylan said. “President Trump has extended the temporary Jones Act exception going on the seventh time. This is the opportunity where we can come together, people of quant, to present our argument even greater before Congress, before Senate, and get that permanent exception we need.”

Both candidates also support improving air connections to Guam and expanding tourism. Moylan highlighted his proposed Pacific Island Flight Alternatives Act, which he said would allow airlines from countries such as Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines to bring visitors to the Marianas and connect them to the U.S. mainland. He also supports a visa-waiver program for visitors from the Philippines.

Limtiaco said she would work with federal agencies, airlines, and industry representatives to find ways to improve air services and address policies that limit competition. She also identified the Philippines as a priority market for a visa-waiver program, citing potential benefits for tourism and the workforce.

The candidates agreed that Guam should receive better access to federal benefits, including Supplemental Security Income and improved Medicaid funding.

Moylan said he would continue pushing legislation to extend SSI to Guam and address limits on federal Medicaid funding. Limtiaco also supports SSI eligibility for Guam residents and removing Guam’s Medicaid funding cap. She said that, if the cap cannot be removed, she would seek adjustments that better reflect the cost of medical care and the number of people needing services.

On the military buildup, Limtiaco said Guam’s civilian community should benefit from federal investments and have a clearer picture of how funding is being spent and when projects will be completed. She identified the power grid, water system, roads, housing, education, and public services as areas needing attention.

Moylan pointed to federal military construction funding and community projects he said he has helped secure, including funding for roads, emergency facilities, and public safety vehicles. He argued that investments supporting infrastructure and pubic services outside military installations also benefit Guam residents.

In their discussion on jobs and workforce needs, Limtiaco identified ship repair as an area that could help diversify Guam’s economy, create jobs, and provide opportunities beyond the military buildup.

Moylan highlighted efforts to extend the H-2B temporary worker program through 2035 and support workforce training. He also pointed to legislation intended to reduce college tuition costs for students in U.S. territories, which he said had passed the House and was awaiting Senate action.

Both candidates said unused federal land should be returned for local use.

In her closing statement, Limtiaco said she would focus on fair treatment in federal programs, stronger infrastructure, and creating more opportunities for Guam’s residents and businesses.

Moylan closed by emphasizing experience, reliability, and following through on commitments. He said he has secured federal investments for Guam but acknowledged that more work remains.

The general election is scheduled for Tuesday.

item.title: CNMI voters head to polls early; runoff plans already underway
item.description: A steady stream of voters lined up Tuesday at the Multi-Purpose Center on Saipan as early voting for the 2026 CNMI general election got underway across the Commonwealth, kicking off a seven-day advance voting period ahead of the Nov. 3 election. item.content:encoded:
A steady stream of voters lined up Tuesday at the Multi-Purpose Center on Saipan as early voting for the 2026 CNMI general election got underway across the Commonwealth, kicking off a seven-day advance voting period ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

Early voting is being conducted on Saipan, Tinian and Rota, giving voters an opportunity to cast ballots before Election Day. On Saipan, voting is taking place at the Multi-Purpose Center, while Tinian voters may vote at the Tinian Youth Center and Rota voters at Northern Marianas College Room B-2.

Commonwealth Election Commission Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna said election officials are prepared for what is expected to be a busy election season and are also developing contingency plans should any race require a runoff election.

"Yes, still we're doing that," Magofna said when asked whether the commission is preparing for a possible runoff.

Under Commonwealth law, a runoff election may be required if no candidate secures the vote threshold necessary for an outright victory. Election officials say the possibility remains particularly significant in the gubernatorial and attorney general races.

The gubernatorial contest featured former Gov. Ralph Torres and running mate Benjamin Jones Jr. against independent tickets headed by Rep. Jonathan "BJ" Attao and House Speaker Edmund Villagomez, as well as former Education Commissioner Lawrence Camacho and former Senate President Edith Deleon Guerrero.

Meanwhile, attorneys Joaquin "Jack" Torres, Jonathan "Robbie" Glass and Michael Evangelista are competing in the attorney general race, which will determine only the second elected attorney general in CNMI history.

Magofna said ballots cast during the general election will be tabulated using voting machines. If a runoff becomes necessary, however, election officials may hand-count ballots because runoff ballots likely would be printed locally.

"The hand counting, we probably will do that during the runoff because we're probably going to print runoff ballots on the island," she said.

Election officials are also reminding voters to bring valid identification, complete the required early-voting application and carefully review both sides of their ballots before casting them.

As of Sept. 19, the Commonwealth had 18,521 registered voters eligible to participate in the election.

Key election dates include the early voting period from Oct. 27 through Nov. 2 and General Election Day on Nov. 3. A runoff election will be scheduled following certification of results if required under Commonwealth election law.

item.title: CPUC to decide Thursday on Eastern Power solar project
item.description: The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission is expected to decide Thursday whether to approve Eastern Power Solutions' proposed multimillion-dollar solar and battery storage project after completing a final review of the agreement and public feedback. item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission is expected to decide Thursday whether to approve Eastern Power Solutions' proposed multimillion-dollar solar and battery storage project after completing a final review of the agreement and public feedback.

Acting Chairman Bruce Camacho said commissioners are conducting one last review of the power purchase agreement and have been evaluating roughly 50 written comments submitted by members of the public.

"The Commission is conducting one final review of the contract and power purchase agreement," Camacho said. "Commissioners have also been sharing the written public comments received individually, and we are carefully reviewing approximately 50 submissions received thus far."

The anticipated decision comes as Eastern Power Solutions has warned that it could withdraw its proposal if regulators fail to act before Oct. 31, citing time-sensitive federal financing incentives tied to the project.

Camacho said the commission has also received a letter from Gov. David Apatang urging regulators to expedite their review. He said the governor reiterated his support for the project during a recent conversation.

"We acknowledge receipt of Gov. Apatang's letter urging the Commission to expedite its review," Camacho said. "I informed him that the Commission intends to convene at the earliest opportunity, Thursday, Oct. 29, to render a decision."

The governor and project supporters have argued that delays could jeopardize financing opportunities and federal tax credits viewed as critical to the project's success.

Among the public comments reviewed by commissioners were concerns about environmental and historic preservation issues. One commenter referenced controversy surrounding Guam's Mangilao solar farm and impacts on Marbo Cave.

Camacho said those concerns are being taken seriously but expressed confidence in the environmental review process.

"These concerns deserve serious consideration, particularly given the scale and long-term nature of the proposed project," he said.

Camacho added that revisions addressing liability and litigation concerns have clarified legal responsibilities between the parties involved. He also noted that any required environmental reviews, consultations and permits must be completed before project activities proceed.

While emphasizing that protecting ratepayers remains the commission's primary responsibility, Camacho said regulators recognize the potential benefits of renewable energy.

"I want to emphasize that the Commission is not attempting to delay this project unnecessarily," he said. "We recognize the potential benefits of renewable energy, including reducing our dependence on imported fossil fuels and providing greater long-term energy price stability for the people of Saipan, Tinian and Rota."

At the same time, Camacho said the proposed agreement represents a significant long-term commitment.

"However, this is a 25-year contractual commitment, and the Commission has a statutory responsibility to ensure that its decision is informed, legally sound and in the best interests of the Commonwealth," he said.

The commission is expected to announce its decision this Thursday.

item.content:encoded:
On May 1, 2023, an unhoused Black man named Jordan Neely boarded the New York City subway. For years, Neely had drawn crowds with his Michael Jackson impersonation, but on that day he was in crisis, shouting threats and frightening fellow passengers.

A white former Marine named Daniel Penny stepped in, putting Neely into a chokehold for six minutes, killing him. Later, a video of the encounter divided the country. To some, Penny was doing what the police weren't there to do. To others, Neely was a victim, another Black man whose life had been treated as disposable.

Journalist Anand Giridharadas spent more than two years investigating what the video couldn't show. He wanted to write a story "that would take us to the heart of America and what it means to live in this country, in this moment." When tragic stories become social media fodder, Giridharadas says, "human beings become caricatures."

In December 2024, Penny was acquitted of criminally negligent homicide after a jury hung on a second degree manslaughter charge and the prosecution dismissed it. Within days of the verdict, Vice President-elect JD Vance invited Penny to the Army-Navy game alongside President-elect Trump. Soon afterward, a Silicon Valley venture capital firm gave him a job.

In his new book, Man in the Mirror: Hope, Struggle, and Belonging in an American City, Giridharadas posits that both men felt let down by the systems that should have protected them.

"I think Jordan Neely had felt abandoned for a very long time, and had reason to feel that way," Giridharadas says. "Daniel Penny would claim that he felt abandoned in terms of law enforcement not being there, and in terms of all the systems that had allowed Jordan Neely to be in that subway car in that condition instead of all of the other conditions that he might have been in had there been a better system of care."

Giridharadas says it's that sense of abandonment that leads people to take matters into their own hands, often with tragic results: "I think it behooves us to think about the condition in which we've left people, this sense of abandonment that we've allowed to be so pervasive that decent people feel like maybe there's no other route for folks besides just DIYing it."

On Jordan Neely's criminal record and the city's attempt at rehabilitation

He had a record of interactions with the police that went back more than a decade. But it was very trivial stuff at the beginning. It was essentially the stuff of what it takes to be homeless in New York, jumping turnstiles, sleeping rough. And then in more recent years, it had gotten more serious and he'd committed a couple of violent crimes, assaults, punching a woman in the face, things like that. And he had gone to Rikers. He'd been charged. And then as part of this alternative to incarceration program — and there are programs like this popping up around the country, where folks get an alternative to going to prison that is considered more restorative, more in line with actually helping people who have substance issues or other issues — he gets to avail of one of these programs. Prosecution, defense, they all agree. And he gets sent to this kind of rehab facility in the Bronx instead of prison. And one day, he just walks out of that facility.

And then, in April 2023, just a few weeks before he died, he is [at] Coney Island, one of the terminal points on the subway system, and he's acting erratically on the platform. Outreach workers try to deal with him to no avail. The cops have some interaction with him, but they don't actually realize that it is the guy who is out with a warrant for his arrest because he walked out of this program. And the outreach workers who were there that night don't quite realize that he's a guy that their agency knows very well, just maybe not those individual workers. And he sort of runs off into the night. And a few weeks later, he's dead on the floor of a different subway car.

On Daniel Penny's origins in West Islip, Long Island

These towns in central Long Island have this very complicated relationship [with New York City]. … On the one hand, it's very out of the city, but it's right there. A lot of people commute in every day for work. Some don't. These are towns that were largely populated by white flight in the last several decades. … In many ways, these are towns that are almost like middle-class refugee camps from the squalor and terror of New York City.

Maybe even understanding immigrant stories is a more helpful framework for understanding these places. … Immigrants have very complicated relationships with the places they leave. We don't think about that with places that are 45 minutes away from a metropolis, but I actually think that is the way to understand the town in which Daniel Penny grew up. … These are communities where there's often a contempt, often barely concealed, for all the people one wanted to get away from, when one left.

I can't know what's in his heart. I didn't sense that kind of sadness or remorse. And not only did I not necessarily pick that up in that brief conversation we had at his victory party a year and a half after the incident, but one of the things that's striking in both the bodycam video on the scene when they first get there, as well as the interrogation ... is that even in those moments, forget remorse, he doesn't even seem to have curiosity about what may have happened to that guy.

He sort of gave the impression of a kind of blankness, ideologically. And that was one of the things that then became very strange, that all these people really wanted him to be their symbol and projected onto him all these ideas. And then he, of course, willingly embraced it. He embraced the money that came from it. And then, most dramatically still, at the end of the case, not only was he content to appear with JD Vance and Donald Trump at the Army-Navy game, but shortly thereafter, he got a job offer that gobsmacked many people. This is someone who, I think, has not graduated from college. He was offered a job as a partner at the venture capital firm in Silicon Valley called Andreessen Horowitz. ... He was made partner on their American dynamism team, which is a team that invests in startups that do weapons systems and drones and other things supposedly in the national interest.

On the politicization of the case and parallels with Luigi Mangione

I had spent the last year and a half hearing Daniel Penny's people make an argument that was basically like, "The system wasn't there, the system wasn't responsive. Daniel Penny stepped into a void and did what he had to do, took matters into his own hands because of this void." And then in the jury deliberations during that moment was the Mangione assassination of Brian Thompson, of United Health Care. And as that case started to become better known, a similar argument started to develop around Luigi Mangione, this time on the parts of the left instead of parts of right that Luigi Mangione was stepping into this void of a cruel healthcare system and stepping in because so many people were abandoned and he felt abandoned. …

And then Hawk Newsome, Black Lives Matter activist in New York, says, yes ... if they're gonna have vigilantes, we need Black vigilantes. But we also need to make our own schools, we need to have our own media, we have to have our own everything.

And I just thought to myself, gosh, is this the last kind of common thread? The idea that you could hear on the far right, the far left, and elsewhere that we're abandoned, the system's rigged, no one's listening, take matters into your own hands. The sense of, somebody step up. Somebody do something.

Anna Bauman and Thea Chaloner produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

item.title: Fed holds interest rates steady even as inflation remains stubborn
item.description: The Federal Reserve opted not to raise interest rates Wednesday, but signaled that it's not retreating from the fight against stubborn inflation. The central bank renewed its pledge to deliver price stability, a goal that's been made more difficult by a spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran.
item.content:encoded:
The Federal Reserve opted not to raise interest rates Wednesday, but signaled that it's not retreating from the fight against stubborn inflation.

The central bank renewed its pledge to deliver price stability, a goal that's been made more difficult by a spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran.

"Inflation remains elevated," the Fed's rate-setting committee acknowledged in a statement .

At its last policy meeting in September, the Fed raised rates for the first time in more than three years. Since then, data has shown inflation has continued to accelerate, with consumer prices in September up 3.7% from a year ago — a bigger annual increase than the previous month.

"It's 'wrong way," says Dan North, a senior economist at the insurance company Allianz Trade. "That inflation line is going up, not down."

The decision not to adjust interest rates comes less than a week before votes are tallied in the midterm election, which may have contributed to the Fed's caution.

"It would be suspicious if there were a hike before the midterm," North said.

After a pause at this week's meeting, Fed policymakers are widely expected to raise their benchmark interest rate at their next meeting in December, in an effort to tamp down demand and bring prices under control.

Two members of the rate-setting committee wanted to move more quickly. Fed governor Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack of the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank voted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point on Wednesday, while a majority of Fed policymakers opted to stand pat.

The Federal Reserve's benchmark rate — currently 3.75 to 4% — helps to establish the cost of other short-term lending for things like credit cards.

Longer-term interest rates are set by the bond market but can also be influenced by Fed decisions. Mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, before easing slightly. The high cost of home loans has been a drag on the housing market, which has been in a slump for the last four years.

Other parts of the economy are less sensitive to rising interest rates. The booming investment in artificial intelligence, for example, shows no sign of slowing down, no matter how much the Fed tries to tap on the brakes.

"The A.I. companies don't care what interest rate they have to pay," North says.

The frenzied push to build A.I. data centers is pushing up prices for construction materials and electronic equipment.

Consumer spending has also remained resilient, fueled in part by upper-income shoppers who benefit from the rising stock market.

That's not the case for less wealthy families, whose wages are not keeping pace with the rising cost of living. Average wages rose just 3% for the 12 months ending in September.

"Lower and middle-income Americans are having a real struggle," says Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. " Their purchasing power is actually declining. And that's a pretty uncomfortable place to be. And that likely goes to explain to a large degree why people don't feel very good about the economy."

item.title: Dolores Huerta, influential labor leader, feminist and civil rights icon, dies at 96
item.description: Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase "Sí, se puede!" that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96. Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.
item.content:encoded:
Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase "Sí, se puede!" that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.

Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.

She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women's rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.

Huerta's resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation's most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to "Yes, it can be done" — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change.

Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. When then-President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and joked that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign.

This year, Huerta sent shockwaves through the Latino community when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement's co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years and long after he died.

From the early 1970s on, Huerta's life partner was Richard Chavez, César's brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages.

Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared that coming forward would compromise her life's work and unravel all the progress made for workers.

When asked during a 2026 interview with the news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: "It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I'll say it that way."

Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who went on to win a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California.

Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism.

Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the farm-rich San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students' poor living conditions.

"I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. "I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children."

Huerta's early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years.

She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year "Delano Grape Strike." With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers.

Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations.

She met U.S. Sen. Robert Kennedy of Massachusetts during his visit to Delano in 1968 and became a volunteer on his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her moments before he was shot.

The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing for farmworkers' rights.

Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating. In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush's opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco.

Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer's baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen, and required more than a dozen blood transfusions. She reached a settlement with the city to resolve her claims.

After a long recovery, Huerta shifted focus and hit the road to campaign for women's rights and encourage Latinas to run for office.

She also campaigned for Democratic Presidents Bill Clinton, Obama and Joe Biden. California Gov. Gavin Newsom considered her a close friend.

Emilio Huerta, one of Dolores' 13 children, once pointed to his mom's courage during an interview, saying it was one of the most significant drivers of her life's work.

"To dedicate your life to building a dream of a union for farmworkers, to take on agriculture, which to this today is still a powerhouse. ... That took a lot of guts," he had said.

Huerta learned the art of lobbying politicians. She secured financial aid for the unemployed and disability insurance for California farmworkers. She spoke out against toxic pesticides, pushed for amnesty for immigrants in the country illegally and fought federal guest worker programs.

By directing nationwide boycotts of grapes and lettuce in the early 1970s, she helped to create the economic pressure and political climate necessary for California to pass what would be the first state law recognizing farmworkers' right to collective bargaining.

Her work earned her many accolades. She was the first Latina to be inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame and she's received nine honorary doctorates from U.S. universities.

Schools are named in her honor in California, Texas and Colorado. Her image graces many murals, and streets bear her name, but she didn't always win favor with more liberal activists.

In 2016 when she endorsed Hillary Clinton instead of Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont in the presidential Democratic primary, actor Rosario Dawson — a Sanders supporter who played Huerta in a 2014 movie about César Chavez — said Huerta had become "an instrument of the establishment."

Dawson and Huerta eventually reconciled.

item.title: What's gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving
item.description: As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP and shared first with NPR, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average.
item.content:encoded:
As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP and shared first with NPR, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average.

The increase during those years is more than twice the overall rate of inflation of 24%, as measured by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index.

What's driving the ramp-up? Food, housing and medical expenses are the biggest chunk, finds the study, which queried 2,538 family caregivers.

The bump in costs comes as family caregivers take on more care and more complicated medical responsibilities at home, says Megan O'Reilly, vice president of governmental affairs at AARP. "The more care that's needed, the more it costs."

And increased spending is only part of the story. The demands of caregiving often require people to reduce their working hours or quit work entirely, the survey finds. It's a double whammy: increased costs on top of lost income.

Meghan Maher has seen that first-hand. Just seven weeks after the birth of her first baby, her mother was diagnosed with advanced cancer. Suddenly, Maher was a "sandwich" caregiver — parent and child needing her at the same time.

At first, she tried to manage it all. She returned to her career in cancer research after maternity leave, but keeping up with the demands of work, her mom and her newborn son was too much.

She shrank her hours to part time. But even that wasn't manageable. There was no way to attend all her mother's appointments, coordinate her care, and also be available for big deadlines on the job.

She quit, and the family's income fell by half. Because her husband had a good job, they weren't struggling, but "it was definitely scary," she says now. As her mom got sicker her parents moved in, increasing the household expenses.

Soon after her mother's death in 2017, her father had a series of major complications from abdominal surgery and was critically ill for months. Maher needed to be by his side during hospital stays, advocating for him on a moment's notice, so now the family also needed to pay for child care. She estimates the cost at about $10,000 a year.

Her father eventually recovered, and the family was able to manage despite the difficulties. Many aren't so lucky.

About half of all family caregivers say they've made major financial sacrifices, according to the AARP report: Working more hours, cutting savings, or even drawing down on money put away for retirement.

Many Americans deal with the cost of care, and more will in the future. About 63 million people now provide ongoing help for a family member or friend — roughly 1 in 4 adults. The need will likely grow: An estimated 70 percent of the people turning 65 today will need some form of help as they age.

Medicare does not pay for routine help either at home or in a facility, and that care is expensive. In 2025, 40 hours of in-home caregiving help a week ran about $72,792 a year, according to the insurance company Genworth, which conducts annual surveys of the cost of care. Skilled nursing costs an average of $115,000 per year for a shared room.

When Maher returned to work, she became a professional death doula. That means she helps clients with the emotional and practical challenges at the end of life. She's self-employed, so she can control her own schedule and limit the number of clients she serves. It allows her the flexibility to help her father as he ages. But her income is half what it would have been in her old career.

With the clients she helps, she sees other ways that care costs pile up. In Florida where she lives, it's routine for chronically ill people to hire an attorney in order to qualify for Medicaid, which unlike Medicare does foot the bill for long-term care. Even though they are eligible for the benefits, the paperwork is so complex that they wind up paying for legal help to navigate it. In Florida, she says, that runs about $6,000.

What she has seen and experienced motivates her to call attention to the caregiving crunch. In May, Maher testified before Congress at a special Senate committee on aging. "Caregiving has also reshaped my professional life," she said to the Senate committee. "The flexibility of self-employment comes with real financial and professional tradeoffs." She was invited by Daughterhood , an organization that offers support and resources for caregivers.

Family caregivers can access some public money, depending on where they live. All states pay some types of family caregivers through Medicaid. In California, for instance, more than 800,000 caregivers earn between $16.90 and $25 an hour for in-home work. Funds for these programs are likely to dwindle due to President Trump's big budget bill that cut nearly $1 trillion out of Medicaid funding over the next decade.

If the person who needs care is eligible for Veterans Administration benefits, they may also be entitled to financial help to cover the cost of caregiving. Like Medicaid, the rules are complex, and many family caregivers hire advocates to advise on eligibility and the application procedure.

The cost of care hasn't been as visible as the cost of gasoline, food and healthcare, says AARP executive vice president Nancy LeaMond. She believes that will change. "When you see the number of people paying this kind of money, I think that'll be an impetus for action in the legislative arena."

In the last few years, Congress has introduced various proposals that could put some money back into the pockets of caregivers, such as allowing caregivers to spend money from their tax-sheltered health savings accounts on their parents' medical expenses. In some states, new rules are already a reality.

Six states now offer tax credits to family caregivers for expenses like retrofitting a home with grab bars or railings, usually between $1,000 and $5,000 a year. Two other states have more limited programs. Last year, two U.S. Senators introduced a bipartisan bill that would establish a similar $5,000 tax credit nationwide.

In 14 states and the District of Columbia, most employers are required to offer paid family and medical leave. Those policies include time off for caregiving for a family member. Another bill introduced into Congress would convert that into a national policy that would require up to 12 weeks of partly paid leave for some workers.

A third proposed federal law would protect the Social Security benefits of caregivers. Under current rules, a person who stops working in order to care full-time for family sees their future Social Security check shrink, because they are no longer earning credits toward retirement. This bill would change the law to continue awarding points to full-time caregivers.

"We spend a lot of time talking to members of Congress, and you can't raise this issue in a meeting without being interrupted by someone telling their own story," says LeaMond. "In time, I believe that will coalesce to support family caregiving."

Kat McGowan is an independent journalist covering adult caregiving who reports the series " What It Takes " for NPR.
